lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.title: Publication, presentation, or reflection: distinguishing similarity from congruence

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: Notice how the explanation names the reason for each step.

items.prompt: Two triangles share two pairs of equal angles. Similar?

steps: The third angles must match too.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: Under a dilation, a line that does not pass through the centre of dilation …
choices: is mapped to a line with slope multiplied by the scale factor
is mapped to a perpendicular line
is mapped to a parallel line

items.prompt: Dilate the point (-2, -5) about the origin with scale factor 3. Give the image.
A figure is dilated so that a side of length 21 becomes a side of length 42. What is the scale factor, and what happens to the figure's area?
choices: scale factor 1/2; the area is multiplied by 4
scale factor 21; the area is multiplied by 4
scale factor 2; the area is multiplied by 2
scale factor 2; the area is multiplied by 4

items.prompt: Triangle ABC has ∠A = 44° and ∠B = 28°. Triangle DEF has ∠D = 44° and ∠E = 28°. Are the triangles similar, and on what grounds?
choices: Yes, by AA similarity: two pairs of congruent angles force the third pair to be congruent as well.
Yes, but only if a pair of corresponding sides is also known to be congruent.
No; angle information alone never establishes similarity.
